title: See it in your room (View in AR) | Verse Engine by Ctruh
description: See it in your room (View in AR) in the Verse Engine by Ctruh docs: what it is, how to use it, and where it fits in your 3D workflow.

docs.article:
See it in your room — View in AR on a phone#

A product-scale scene (a chair, a lamp, a watch, a chess set) can be placed on a real table from its share link. Nothing to install: the scene's own page shows View in AR on phones that can do it.

What the visitor gets#

PhoneWhat happens on View in AR
Android, Chrome (and other WebXR-capable browsers)The page opens a WebXR AR session. A white ring follows the surfaces the camera finds; tap places the object on it, one finger turns it, pinch resizes it (the readout shows the factor), Reset picks it up again, Exit AR returns to the page. The object is the same streamed scene the page was showing — it keeps streaming detail while you look at it, and the room's light level nudges its exposure.
iPhone / iPad, SafariThe control is Apple's AR Quick Look link: Safari opens the scene's .usdz in AR with its own placement, scale and share sheet.
Desktop, or a phone without ARNo control is shown.

The control appears only for product-scale scenes: the compile-time staging says kind: "object", or — for open / pre-kind scenes — the scene is at most 6 m across. Interiors are walked through (and viewed in a headset), never placed on a table.

What the server builds#

When a scene compiles, the ingest route also writes ingest/<id>.usdz — the iOS AR Quick Look package — from the prepared GLB, right before the source file is deleted. It is served exactly like the scene's other artifacts (model/vnd.usdz+zip, immutable, same visibility: a private scene's package needs the owner's cookie or the share token; it follows the scene's version with ?v=), and the finished job record says so:

Code
{ "status": "done", "vpkUrl": "…/ingest/chair-1a2b3c4d5e6f.vpk",
  "arUrl":  "https://HOST/ingest/chair-1a2b3c4d5e6f.usdz",
  "ar":     { "bytes": 13122418, "triangles": 76920, "textures": 9, "resized": 0, "seconds": 0.05 } }

or, when there is none, why: "ar": { "skipped": "an interior is walked through, not placed in a room" }, "… over the 150 MB AR cap", "… over the 5 M AR cap".

Caps (web/playground/usdz.mjs, USDZ_LIMITS): a prepared GLB of at most 150 MB and 5 M triangles; PNG textures wider than 2048 px are downsampled in the package (JPEGs stay as encoded — verse-prepare already caps them at 4096 on ingest). The three bundled demos convert in under 0.1 s each (chess set 76.9 k tris → 12.5 MB; marble bust 17.5 k tris → 6.5 MB; antique camera 20 k tris → 18.7 MB); the package is text USDA plus the images, so it is larger than the .vpk. VERSE_AR=0 turns the packaging off on a server.

The converter is pure Node — no native dependency, nothing to install on the server — and the packages pass Apple's own validator (usdchecker --arkit, which macOS ships). What it carries: every mesh instance with its world transform, vertex normals and st texcoords, UsdPreviewSurface materials with base colour, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive textures, alpha blend / mask, double-sided. What it leaves out (honest list): animations and skins (bind pose only), KHR_texture_transform, vertex colours, sparse accessors, KTX2 textures (factors only — the compact atlas tier is not an image Quick Look reads).

For developers#

  • API: arUrl / ar on the finished job record (api.md § GET /v1/ingest/<job>); the file itself at GET /ingest/<id>.usdz.
  • SDK: verse.scenes.arUrl(id, { share?, version? }) builds the link — put it in <a rel="ar" href="…"><img src="poster.png"></a> on your own page and Safari opens it in AR (sdk.md).
  • Embed: the viewer shows its own View in AR control inside the frame; the stage event's ar field tells your page which path the device has ("webxr", "quicklook" or null), viewer.enterAR() starts it and ar events report what happened (embed-sdk.md). WebXR needs a tap inside the frame: a programmatic enterAR() on Android may report state: "blocked"; the in-frame button always works.
  • Links: nothing to add — the share link shows the control on its own.

How the WebXR path renders (and its honest limits)#

The session reuses the headset plumbing (web/playground/xr.js): the engine's mono loop is suspended, every XR frame's camera pose crosses to the render worker as an xr-frame (the same pose for both "eyes" — the stereo path is the engine's one external-camera path), and a WebGL2 presenter on the main thread samples the left half of the engine canvas into the XRWebGLLayer. The camera feed shows through where the engine painted its backdrop: the session sets the solid backdrop (?bg='s lane) to a chroma key (#00ff00, pure green) and the presenter keys it to alpha 0. That is the v1 of a transparent clear — exact on the flat backdrop, with a narrow halo possible on anti-aliased silhouettes against it; a true alpha render target is the follow-up (backlog). Placement is a model matrix folded into the view matrix (the object's base centre on the hit pose, the turn and the pinch scale), so the engine streams and culls exactly as it does on the page. Light estimation (XRLightProbe's primary intensity) nudges the engine's exposure by at most ±1.5 EV, smoothed.

Offered on browsers with WebGPU only — the stereo path renders the session; the WebGL2 build shows no WebXR control (iOS Safari uses Quick Look on every device). Temporal mode (?temporal=) is refused like VR.

What is proven, and what needs a phone#

web/test/fix-verify-ar.mjs (ports 8820–8829) proves, headlessly: the package is built through the real ingest route, is a valid USDZ (stored entries, 64-byte alignment, CRCs, the USDA first), references every material and texture, is under the cap, passes usdchecker --arkit; an interior gets none; the control is an <a rel="ar"> with its <img> on an emulated iPhone and absent on desktop; with navigator.xr stubbed, the WebXR button appears, requestSession asks for immersive-ar with hit-test required and dom-overlay + light-estimation optional, the renderer switches to the AR clear mode (suspend → AR-size resize → chroma key backdrop), stubbed frames produce xr-frame poses, a tap places, a pinch scales, exit restores everything; the embed's stage.ar and enterAR().

Only a phone can prove that ARCore finds the plane and the keyed frame composites cleanly over the camera feed, that Safari hands the link to AR Quick Look and places the object at true scale, and what real-room light estimates look like. Test plan for the first device pass: open /view?vpk=ingest/demo-chess-set.vpk on an Android phone in Chrome → View in AR → place on a table (the board should be 55 cm across); on an iPhone → View in AR → Quick Look opens; both paths on a private scene with ?share=.
